questions.topic: What the weight of a script bundle is made of
questions.learningObjective: identify the contributions that make up a shipped script file
questions.stem: A page ships 480 kilobytes of script and the network panel shows it arriving as one file. Which of these is inside that 480 kilobytes?

options.text: The module code, the values the code holds, and the runtime it needs
Only the module code, because data and runtime are fetched at run time
options.misconception: believes data and the runtime are always fetched after the file

options.text: Only the code the entry module imports, not the modules it imports
options.misconception: believes a file contains only the modules named in the first import

options.text: The compiled code alone, because names and comments are dropped by the compiler
options.misconception: believes the compiler is the step that removes names and comments

questions.explanation: A bundle is everything needed to run, flattened into one file: the code of every module that survived, the constants and tables those modules define, and whatever library support the target needs. That is why a file can be far larger than the code anyone wrote, and why a single large dependency moves the number more than any amount of local tidying. questions.topic: What lets a build drop an unused module
questions.learningObjective: state the condition under which an unused module may be dropped
questions.stem: A package ships 300 modules, the application imports two of them, and the built file still contains all 300. What decides whether the other 298 can be removed?

options.text: Whether the package declares its modules free of side effects, so removing one is safe
Whether the two imported modules are written with const rather than let
options.misconception: believes a keyword choice decides whether a module can be dropped

options.text: Whether the build can minify every module, since minified code is droppable
options.misconception: believes minifying a module makes it safe to remove

options.text: Whether the package lists its modules in one entry file, so nothing is ambiguous
options.misconception: believes a single entry file is what makes dropping safe

questions.topic: How a wait after the last keystroke shapes a request curve
questions.learningObjective: trace the calls a delayed search makes over a burst of keystrokes
questions.stem: A search box runs `runSearch()` 300 ms after the user stops typing, cancelling any earlier wait. Keystrokes arrive at 0, 100, 200 and 300 ms, and the run is watched until 900 ms. How many times does it run, and when?

options.text: Once, at 600 ms, because each keystroke replaces the wait before it
Four times, at 300, 400, 500 and 600 ms, because each keystroke starts a wait
options.misconception: believes several pending waits run one after another instead of being replaced

options.text: Twice, at 0 and 300 ms, because the wait is measured from the first keystroke
options.misconception: believes the wait is counted from the first keystroke rather than the last

options.text: Never, because each keystroke restarts the wait before it can ever finish
options.misconception: believes replacing a pending wait also cancels the search it stood for

questions.topic: A token bucket and the requests it turns away
questions.learningObjective: trace how many requests a token bucket serves in a burst
questions.stem: A route serves a request with `if (tokens < 1) return 429;` from a bucket that holds 5 places and gains one place back every second, up to that cap. Eight requests arrive inside the same second. How many are served, and what happens to the rest?

options.text: 5 are served, and the other 3 are refused with a hint to retry later
All 8 are served, because the bucket refills once for the whole group
options.misconception: believes a refill makes places available to every waiting request at once

options.text: 5 are served, and the other 3 wait until places free up and are then run
options.misconception: believes a token bucket holds requests rather than only places

options.text: 1 is served, because the bucket holds one place however many it was given
options.misconception: believes the configured capacity is a rate rather than a store of places

questions.explanation: The bucket starts with five places, and each of the eight requests that arrives inside the same second takes one if there is one left. The first five succeed and the bucket is empty, and because the whole burst lands before any second has passed there are no places back yet, so the last three are refused. A token bucket refuses rather than queues, which is what keeps a busy client from accumulating a backlog of work the server never intended to accept. The store-versus-rate confusion is common because the number 5 reads like a rate, and the difference decides whether a burst of eight is mostly served or mostly refused.
questions.hint: Ask whether a place comes back before the last of the eight requests has arrived.

questions.learningObjective: count the queries a lookup inside a loop produces
questions.stem: A page loads three orders. The code runs one statement for the orders and then, inside the loop over them, one statement per order to get its customer name. How many statements reach the database for this one page load?

options.text: Four, because the loop adds one statement for each order it visits
Three, because the order statement and the customer ones share a round trip
options.misconception: believes a statement inside a loop reuses the previous round trip

options.text: One, because the customer name is joined onto the order rows in the same statement
options.misconception: believes a loop over rows does not produce further statements by itself

options.text: Two, because the loop's customer statements are sent as one batched statement
options.misconception: believes statements issued in a loop are combined into one by the driver

The cost grows with the page, which is the whole point: a page of fifty orders costs fifty-one round trips, and most of the time is spent waiting rather than working. One joined statement, or one statement asking for every customer the page needs and matching the names afterwards, turns the growth into a constant. The batching belief is worth testing directly on a real loop, because drivers do not merge statements that were issued separately.
questions.hint: Add the one statement before the loop to the count made inside it.

questions.stem: A list holds ids 1 to 10 in order and the page size is 5. Page two is fetched with `rows.slice(5, 10)`. Then id 3 is deleted and page two is fetched the same way. Which ids come back the second time?

options.text: 7, 8, 9 and 10, because the deletion moved every later id one place up
6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, because a slice of five always yields five rows
options.misconception: believes a slice always returns as many rows as its length asks for

options.text: 8, 9 and 10, because the deleted id is also missing from the rows after it
options.misconception: believes a deletion shortens the list by more than the one row removed

options.text: 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, because the offset is counted from the top of the list
options.misconception: believes the offset counts the page rather than the rows to skip

questions.explanation: After the deletion the list is 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, so skipping five rows lands on 7 and the page is 7, 8, 9, 10, only four rows because the list is one shorter. The row with id 6 has moved into page one, so anyone reading page one and then page two never sees it at all, and a reader who fetched page one before the deletion sees 6 twice. A cursor that names the last key of the previous page keeps pointing at the same row however many rows come and go before it.

questions.learningObjective: decide whether a script address matches a policy source
questions.stem: A policy is set with `res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy', "script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com")` and the page is at `https://app.example.com/dashboard`. One tag has `src="https://cdn.example.com.evil.net/lib.js"`. Does the policy allow it?

options.text: No, because the host must equal the allowed host or sit directly under it
Yes, because the host contains the allowed host as a run of characters
options.misconception: believes a host containing the allowed name matches that source

options.text: Yes, because the address uses the same scheme as the allowed source
options.misconception: believes matching the scheme is enough to satisfy a host source

options.text: No, because the host ends in net rather than in com at its end
options.misconception: believes a host must end with the same final label as the allowed host

questions.explanation: A host source matches when the address's host is that host exactly or a subdomain of it, judged at the label boundary, so app.example.com is under example.com and cdn.example.com.evil.net is not under cdn.example.com: the allowed name there is in the middle of a longer name owned by someone else. Comparing characters anywhere in the string is what lets that address through, and it is the most common way a policy written by hand is defeated. The same mistake in a server allowlist is a real vulnerability, so the rule worth remembering is the label boundary, not the substring.

options.text: A hashed value, because the build hashes every long string it writes in
options.misconception: believes a build step automatically hashes any secret it inserts

options.text: Name that one host in the script source list, and keep the header in place
Move the report tool's address into a connect source list instead
options.misconception: believes a connect source permits a script to be loaded and run

options.text: Allow any host with a wildcard so the report tool is never blocked again

options.misconception: believes rendering the control as disabled stops a second submission

options.text: Remove the click handler once it has run, so a second click finds nothing
options.misconception: believes the click path is the only route that can submit the form

options.text: Add a delay to the response so the second request arrives after the first
options.misconception: believes a slower response prevents a duplicate write

questions.learningObjective: choose what a readiness check must verify to be worth having
questions.stem: A service reports healthy from a handler that returns 200 as soon as the process answers, while its database refuses every connection. What does that check fail to tell the operator?

options.text: Whether the service can do its work, since a running process may serve nothing useful
How fast the process answers, because a slow answer is a different fault
options.misconception: believes a readiness check must report response time

options.text: Which user is asking, because the answer should differ per account
options.misconception: believes a health endpoint should be scoped to the caller

options.text: Whether the build is current, because a stale build is a health problem
options.misconception: believes a health check should verify the deployed version

A process whose database is unreachable is alive and useless, and a readiness check that says otherwise keeps traffic going to it, so requests fail in a way that looks like an application bug. The useful check exercises the dependency the work needs, with a short timeout, and reports the reason so the difference between a slow answer and a broken one is visible. There is a separate liveness question, which is whether to restart the process, and conflating the two is how a service gets restarted for a database outage it did not cause.
questions.hint: Ask what a request served by this instance would need in order to succeed.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What promising that a file never changes does and does not promise
questions.learningObjective: explain the promise an immutable cache directive makes and its limit
questions.stem: Explain what `immutable` promises a browser about a cached file, what it does not promise, and what happens if the bytes at that address are later replaced.

answer.exemplar: The directive is a statement to the browser about how long a stored copy stays good: during its freshness period the copy may be used without asking again, and it is not revalidated even when a reload is requested, so the bytes a file had when it was stored are the bytes the browser keeps serving. What it does not promise is anything about the origin; it is an assertion the server makes, not a guarantee the file system can enforce, and it says nothing about the first load, about other caches, or about the address being permanent. That is the limit, and it is why the directive is safe only on a name that changes when the content does. If the bytes at the same address are later replaced, a browser still holding a fresh copy keeps serving the old ones for the rest of the period and never finds out, so the fix is not to shorten the period afterwards but to make the new content arrive at a new address, which is what a content hash in the file name does. Serving the old file from a cache is not a cache bug; the mistake was promising permanence for an address that did not have it.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to separate what the directive instructs the browser to do, which is skip revalidation for the freshness period, from what it guarantees, which is nothing at all about the server's future behaviour. The consequence of replacing the bytes at the same address has to be stated plainly, and the resolution named as a new address rather than a shorter period.
questions.hint: Separate what the browser is told to do from what the server actually promises.

questions.stem: Explain what a build must be told before it can leave an imported but unused module out, and what goes wrong when it is told the wrong thing in either direction.

answer.exemplar: A module that is imported and whose exports are never read is not necessarily dead, because running a module can change something outside it: it can register a handler, patch another library, start a timer, or write to a shared store. A build may only leave it out when running it would have changed nothing, so the only reliable statement about that is the package saying so, and silence has to be read as the cautious answer rather than as permission. Claiming no module has effects when some do produces a bundle that is missing code the page needed, and the failure appears as something not working with no mention of the build in the trace at all. Claiming every module has effects when most do produces a bundle that keeps everything, so a package shipping three hundred modules and being asked for two still carries three hundred, which is the situation a person usually discovers by looking at a size and wondering what is in it. Neither keyword choice nor the file layout tells a build this, and minifying does not either, since shortening a module's text says nothing about what running it would do. The declaration is a small piece of information a maintainer writes once per package, and it is the only thing that lets a build do the work.

An answer that says only that unused code should be removed has not addressed why a build is not allowed to remove it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens merely by importing a module, before any of its exports are read.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why the two health questions have to be separate
questions.learningObjective: explain what each health check decides and what confusion between them costs
questions.stem: Explain why a service needs one check that asks whether to restart it and another that asks whether to send it traffic, and what goes wrong if the two are merged.

answer.exemplar: The two checks answer different questions because the actions taken from their answers are different and neither answer is right for the other's question. Liveness asks whether this process is working at all, and a negative answer means it should be replaced, so the check must be cheap and must not depend on anything outside the process, or a blip elsewhere will have every instance restarting at once. Readiness asks whether this instance can usefully serve a request, which means exercising the dependencies the work needs: if the database refuses connections, the instance is alive and useless, and it should be taken out of rotation rather than restarted. Merging them is expensive in a specific way. Report a failing database as a liveness failure and the platform restarts every instance in turn while the database is still down, so one outage becomes a restart loop, and the instances come back still unable to serve and get restarted again, which fills the logs and hides the actual cause. Report the failure as readiness and the traffic moves elsewhere while the database is repaired, which is the outcome that was wanted. The other half of keeping them apart is that readiness has to say what failed and why, since a bare failure leaves an operator with an instance that is refusing work and no indication whether to repair a dependency, raise a limit, or look at the code.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to state the two questions, tie each to the action taken from it, and describe the restart loop that merging them produces. An answer that only says one is about the process and the other is about the service has not said what the difference costs when it is ignored.
questions.hint: Ask what is done with each answer, and what happens if the wrong one is used.

questions.topic: What a limit is for and what a caller does next
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose of a rate limit and the caller's part in it
questions.stem: A route refuses a request because that caller has asked too often. What is the limit for, and what should the caller do?

options.text: Keeping one caller from crowding out others, and waiting before retrying
Making the route slower on purpose, so that callers learn to stop
options.misconception: believes a limit is meant to discourage the caller

options.text: Charging the caller for the requests, so retrying is what adds cost
options.misconception: believes a limit exists to bill the caller

options.text: Keeping the route's own memory small, so callers should send less
options.misconception: believes a limit is a measure of the route's memory

questions.explanation: A shared service has a finite amount of capacity and no way to tell a legitimate caller from one that has stopped caring, so the limit exists to stop any one caller from using all of it, which is what makes the service unusable for everyone else. That is why a refusal carries a hint about when to come back rather than being silent, and why a caller that backs off and retries is behaving correctly while one that retries immediately is not, having turned its own refusal into extra load. The purpose is fairness between callers, and the failure it produces for the caller that ignores it is being refused, which is a cost it brought on itself.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the other callers when one of them sends without stopping.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A cache key that leaves out part of the request
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a cache key that cannot tell two different requests apart
questions.stem: A cache stores responses under the path alone, so `/report?month=1` and `/report?month=2` share one entry. What goes wrong, and what must a key therefore include?

options.text: A reader asking for one month can be served the other month's answer
Both are refused, since one address may only have one stored answer
options.misconception: believes a shared key makes the second request impossible

options.text: The newer answer replaces the older, so only the later request succeeds
options.misconception: believes a shared key means only one of the two is ever served

options.text: Nothing, since a query is a hint and the two requests are one request
options.misconception: believes a query never changes what is being asked for

questions.explanation: A key has to distinguish two requests that deserve different answers, and a path does not when the query is what selects the data, so whichever request came first fills the entry and everyone after it is served that answer until it expires. A report for the wrong month is the visible symptom, and the more serious one is any key of this shape that carries a permission, where one reader is handed another's answer. The query is part of what is being asked for, so it belongs in the key, and the same applies to the name of the format being asked in, which is why a key is built from the whole request rather than from its address.
questions.hint: Ask what part of the request decides which answer is correct, and whether the key includes it.
